segments.text: This is a download from BBC Learning English. To find out more, visit our website.

segments.speaker: Sam
segments.text: Hello, this is 6 Minute English from BBC Learning English. I'm Sam.

segments.speaker: Neil
segments.text: And I'm Neil.

segments.speaker: Sam
segments.text: There was a huge crowd of people waiting at the train station this morning, Neil.

segments.speaker: Sam
segments.text: When the train finally arrived, everyone rushed in and I couldn't find a seat.

segments.speaker: Sam
segments.text: I hate crowds.

segments.speaker: Neil
segments.text: But you love going to the football match on Saturday.

segments.speaker: Sam
segments.text: Ah, well that's different. More like a big group of friends.

segments.speaker: Neil
segments.text: Well, whether it's sporting events, train stations or political protests,

segments.speaker: Neil
segments.text: crowds that's large groups of people who gather together for a shared activity are a feature of life.

segments.speaker: Neil
segments.text: For some, crowds create feelings of excitement and a sense of community,

segments.speaker: Neil
segments.text: while for others they feel uncomfortable, confusing or even dangerous.

segments.speaker: Neil
segments.text: So why is that?

segments.speaker: Sam
segments.text: In this programme we'll be discussing the role of crowds in modern life,

segments.speaker: Sam
segments.text: asking why they evoke different reactions in people.

segments.speaker: Sam
segments.text: And as usual, we'll be learning some new vocabulary as well.

segments.speaker: Sam
segments.text: But first, I have a question for you, Neil.

segments.speaker: Sam
segments.text: The biggest crowd in history happened in 2019

segments.speaker: Sam
segments.text: when over 200 million people gathered in the northern Indian city of Allahabad.

segments.speaker: Sam
segments.text: But what did so many people come together for?

segments.speaker: Sam
segments.text: Was it a a cricket match b a religious festival or c an election

segments.speaker: Neil
segments.text: Well I know Indians love cricket but I doubt 200 million people would fit into a stadium

segments.speaker: Neil
segments.text: so I'll guess it's C an election.

segments.speaker: Sam
segments.text: OK Neil, we'll find out the answer later in the programme.

segments.speaker: Sam
segments.text: People gathering for a cricket match or a music concert are usually happy events.

segments.speaker: Sam
segments.text: But crowds can have a darker side as well.

segments.speaker: Sam
segments.text: They can become out of control and sometimes even violent.

segments.speaker: Sam
segments.text: Here's psychologist Professor John Drury discussing this idea with Anand Jagassia,

segments.speaker: Sam
segments.text: presenter of the BBC World Service programme, appropriately named Crowd Science.

segments.speaker: Sam
segments.text: When people get together in a crowd, they regress psychologically,

segments.speaker: Sam
segments.text: their thinking is more primitive, they become more gullible,

segments.speaker: Sam
segments.text: and that's also associated with a supposed tendency towards violence as well.

segments.speaker: Sam
segments.text: But according to John, the idea of mob mentality,

segments.speaker: Sam
segments.text: that people in crowds are irrational and prone to destructive behaviour

segments.speaker: Sam
segments.text: just isn't backed up by research.

segments.speaker: Neil
segments.text: One view is that when people get together in a crowd, they become irrational.

segments.speaker: Neil
segments.text: Psychologically speaking, they regress.

segments.speaker: Neil
segments.text: They return to a less advanced, more primitive way of behaving.

segments.speaker: Neil
segments.text: They may also become more gullible,

segments.speaker: Neil
segments.text: an adjective meaning easily tricked or willing to believe everything someone says.

segments.speaker: Sam
segments.text: Connected to this is the phrase mob mentality,

segments.speaker: Sam
segments.text: the tendency of people in a group to behave

segments.speaker: Sam
segments.text: in the same way as others in the group,

segments.speaker: Sam
segments.text: rather than as individuals In crowds people may do things they would never do alone like steal or use violence

segments.speaker: Neil
segments.text: But according to Professor Drury in reality it not mob mentality and violence but rather feelings

segments.speaker: Neil
segments.text: of safety and togetherness that actually characterise crowds. And according to Dr Anne Templeton,

segments.speaker: Neil
segments.text: another expert on crowd psychology from the University of Edinburgh, that's especially true

segments.speaker: Neil
segments.text: when you identify with the other people in a crowd.

segments.speaker: Neil
segments.text: Here's Dr Templeton explaining more to BBC World Service programme CrowdScience.

segments.speaker: Neil
segments.text: The more people feel like they are part of a group with others in the crowd,

segments.speaker: Neil
segments.text: the more enjoyable experience they have.

segments.speaker: Neil
segments.text: There's a correlation between having that social identification and feeling safer.

segments.speaker: Neil
segments.text: So often if we feel like we are in a group with others, we expect them to look after us.

segments.speaker: Neil
segments.text: The flip side of that is when you don't feel as much part of the group

segments.speaker: Neil
segments.text: and you're not having this positive experience.

segments.speaker: Neil
segments.text: Dr Templeton thinks there is a correlation that's a connection or a link

segments.speaker: Neil
segments.text: between being among people who share your values and feeling safe.

segments.speaker: Neil
segments.text: Football fans cheer their team on by wearing the same colours and singing the same songs

segments.speaker: Neil
segments.text: and this works as a kind of glue, bonding the crowd together and making them feel safe.

segments.speaker: Sam
segments.text: The disadvantage of this, however, is when you don't feel part of the crowd you're with.

segments.speaker: Sam
segments.text: Dr Templeton calls this the flip side, the opposite, less good or less pleasant aspect of something.

segments.speaker: Neil
segments.text: In today world crowds are important because of the feeling of power they give us It one thing sitting alone shouting at the news on television but it something else altogether to march on a political protest

segments.speaker: Neil
segments.text: with hundreds of demonstrators feeling that together you could change the world.

segments.speaker: Neil
segments.text: Maybe that's what everyone was doing in 2019, Sam.

segments.speaker: Sam
segments.text: Right. In my question, I asked you why 200 million people

segments.speaker: Sam
segments.text: gathered in the Indian city of Allahabad in 2019.

segments.speaker: Neil
segments.text: I guessed it was to vote in an election, was I right?

segments.speaker: Sam
segments.text: You were wrong, I'm afraid, Neil.

segments.speaker: Sam
segments.text: In fact, the biggest crowd in history had gathered for a Hindu religious festival,

segments.speaker: Sam
segments.text: the Kamb Mela, which 220 million people attended over 50 days.

segments.speaker: Sam
segments.text: OK, let's recap the vocabulary we've learned from this programme on crowds.

segments.speaker: Sam
segments.text: Large numbers of people who gather together for a shared reason.

segments.speaker: Neil
segments.text: To regress means return to less advanced, more primitive behaviours. Regress is the opposite of progress.

segments.speaker: Sam
segments.text: Someone who is gullible is easily tricked and will believe anything people say.

segments.speaker: Neil
segments.text: The phrase mob mentality describes the tendency of people in a group to behave in ways that conform with others in the group rather than as individuals.

segments.speaker: Sam
segments.text: A correlation is a connection or a link between two things.

segments.speaker: Neil
segments.text: And finally, the flip side of something means those aspects of it which are less obvious, good or pleasant.

segments.speaker: Neil
segments.text: The flip side of this programme is that once again our six minutes are up.

segments.speaker: Neil
segments.text: Bye for now.

segments.speaker: Sam
segments.text: Bye bye.
